lessons.title: Lesson 1: Mapping a process you repeat
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draw a repeated business process as a list of steps from start to finish.
This lesson builds toward: Given a process you repeat every week, you will map it as steps from start to finish, marking each as copying, decision or writing, with anything AI got wrong corrected.
Before you automate anything, write it down. A workflow is the steps a piece of work goes through from start to finish. Example, a new customer inquiry: the form arrives, you copy the details into a spreadsheet, you write a reply, you add a follow-up reminder.
Pick a process that happens often, follows the same steps each time, and wastes your time with copying, pasting or retyping. Those are the best ones to automate.
AI can help you map it. Describe what you do in your own words and ask: "Turn this into a numbered workflow. Mark which steps are copying information, which need a decision, and which need writing."
Step by step:
- Choose a process you do at least weekly.
- Describe it to an AI assistant in your own words.
- Ask for a numbered workflow, marking copying, decision and writing steps.
- Check the map against what you really do and fix it.
Words to know:
- Workflow: the steps a piece of work goes through from start to finish.
- Automate: set a computer to do a repeated job without you doing each step.
Try it now: Map one process you repeat weekly with AI's help. Mark each step as copying, decision or writing, and correct anything AI got wrong.
You can now map a repeated business process as clear steps.

options: The steps work goes through from start to finish
check.why: A workflow lists each step of a process in order.

check.q: AI's map of your order process leaves out the step where you check stock. What do you do?
options: Use the map as it is
check.why: You know your process best, so you correct AI's map.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Triggers and actions
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your workflow map into a trigger and a list of actions.
This lesson builds toward: Given your workflow map, you will write the workflow as a trigger and a list of actions, with the AI action and the approval step marked.
Every automation has one trigger and one or more actions. The trigger is the event that starts it: "a new form response", "a new email with the word invoice", "a new paid order". The actions are what happens next: "add a row to a spreadsheet", "send me a message", "create a calendar event".
Copying steps become actions easily. Writing steps can become AI actions. Decision steps usually stay with you, or become an approval step where the automation waits for your yes.
No-code tools such as Zapier, Make and Microsoft Power Automate connect apps you already use with triggers and actions. Most have free plans with limits; check each tool's pricing page for what is included today.
Step by step:
- Find the event that starts your workflow: that is the trigger.
- Turn each copying step into an action.
- Turn writing steps into AI actions.
- Turn decision steps into an approval step or keep them manual.
- Write it as: When [trigger], then [action 1], [action 2]...
Words to know:
- Trigger: the event that starts an automation.
- Action: a step the automation does after the trigger.
- No-code tool: a tool that lets you build automations by clicking and choosing, not programming.
Official sources:
- Zapier: Pricing
- Make: Pricing
Try it now: Write your workflow as "When [trigger], then [actions]". Mark which action is AI and where you want an approval step.
You can now describe any automation as a trigger plus actions, with decisions kept under your control.

check.q: In "When a payment arrives, send a receipt", what is the action?
check.why: The action is what happens after the trigger.

check.q: One step in your workflow is deciding whether to give a refund. How do you handle it?
options: Keep it as an approval step for you
check.why: Decision steps become approvals or stay with you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Building your first no-code automation
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Build a working automation that moves form answers into a spreadsheet and notifies you.
This lesson builds toward: Using a no-code tool's free plan, you will build an automation that moves form answers into a spreadsheet and notifies you, tested with made-up data and working.
Start with a simple, safe automation: when someone fills in your inquiry form (for example a Google Form or Microsoft Form), add their answers to a spreadsheet and send you a notification. Nothing goes to the customer yet.
In your no-code tool, create a new automation, choose the form app as the trigger, connect your account, and pick the form. Then add an action for the spreadsheet, and match each form question to a column. Add a second action to email or message you.
Test it with a fake inquiry using a made-up name like "Test Customer". Check that the row appears in the right columns and that you got the message. Only then turn it on.
Step by step:
- Make a short inquiry form with name, email and request.
- In the no-code tool, choose the form as the trigger.
- Add a spreadsheet action and match questions to columns.
- Add an action to notify you.
- Test with "Test Customer" data, check results, then turn it on.
Words to know:
- Connect an account: give the automation tool permission to use one of your apps.
- Field mapping: matching each piece of information to where it should go, like a form question to a spreadsheet column.
Try it now: Build the form-to-spreadsheet-plus-notification automation in a no-code tool's free plan. Test it with made-up data and confirm it works.
You can now build and test a simple no-code automation between apps you use.

check.q: What is field mapping in a no-code tool?
options: Matching each piece of information to where it goes
Drawing a map of your shop
check.why: Field mapping sends each answer to the right column.

check.q: Your automation is built. What do you do before switching it on?
options: Test it with made-up data like "Test Customer"
check.why: Testing with made-up data finds problems without risk.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Add AI and keep control

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Adding an AI step
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Add an AI action that drafts a reply or sorts a request.
This lesson builds toward: Given your working automation, you will add an AI step that drafts a reply or sorts a request and sends it to you, with clear rules, tested on three different requests and no private data passing through.
Many no-code tools let you add an AI action: send text to an AI model with an instruction and get its answer back as part of the automation. Common uses: sort an inquiry into a category, pull out key details, or draft a reply. On some tools the AI step is only on paid plans (when checked in October 2026, Zapier's AI steps needed a paid plan); check the pricing page. If yours is not included, have the automation send you the request and paste it into a free chat assistant yourself.
Write the AI instruction carefully, like a reusable prompt: "Read this customer request. Reply in under 100 words, friendly and clear. Only use the business details given here: [hours, services]. Never quote a price. If unsure, write [CHECK]."
Send the AI's draft to YOU, not to the customer. Think about what customer information passes to the AI service; check the tool's data and privacy terms, and do not send card numbers, ID numbers or health details through it.
Step by step:
- Add an AI action after the spreadsheet step.
- Write a careful instruction with rules and your business facts.
- Pass in only the request text the AI needs.
- Send the AI's draft to yourself for review.
- Test with three different made-up requests.
Words to know:
- AI action: a step in an automation that sends text to an AI and uses its answer.
- Data terms: the rules for how a tool stores and uses the information you send it.
Official sources:
- Zapier: Pricing (AI steps and plan limits)
Try it now: Add an AI step to your automation that drafts a reply and sends it to you. Test it with three different made-up requests and note any mistakes.
You can now add an AI step to an automation with clear rules and private data kept out.

check.q: Which rule belongs in an AI step's instruction?
options: "Only use the facts given; never quote a price"
check.why: Clear rules keep AI drafts accurate and safe.

check.q: Your form asks for a card number. What do you do about the AI step?
options: Leave that field out of what the AI step receives
check.why: Card numbers and private data should not pass through the AI step.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Agents and guardrails
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide what an AI agent may do alone and what needs your approval.
This lesson builds toward: For your automation or any AI agent, you will write a guardrail list of what it may do alone and what always needs your approval, with sending to customers and spending money always needing approval.
An AI agent is given a goal and plans and takes several steps on its own, such as searching, filling in forms, or using your apps. Agents can save time, but they can also make mistakes quickly and at scale.
Guardrails are the limits you set. A simple rule: an agent may read, sort and draft on its own, but it must get your approval before it sends anything to a customer, spends money, deletes anything, changes prices or signs up for anything. Give it access only to the apps and folders it needs.
Keep a record of what the agent did (most tools have a history or log) and start with small, low-risk tasks. Add more freedom only after it has worked well for a while.
Step by step:
- List what the agent will do.
- Mark each action: allowed alone, or needs your approval.
- Require approval for sending, spending, deleting, pricing and sign-ups.
- Limit its access to only the apps and folders it needs.
- Check its history or log regularly.
Words to know:
- AI agent: an AI tool that takes several steps on its own toward a goal.
- Guardrail: a limit that stops an automation or agent doing something risky.
- Log: a record of what an automation or agent did and when.
Try it now: Write a guardrail list for your automation: what it may do alone, and the five things that always need your approval. Add an approval step if your tool supports one.
You can now set guardrails so automations and agents never act on risky steps without you.

check.q: What is a guardrail in an automation?
options: A limit that stops risky actions
check.why: Guardrails stop the automation from doing risky things alone.

check.q: An agent tool asks for access to all your folders and your bank. What do you give it?
options: Only the apps and folders it needs
check.why: Least access limits the damage if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Testing, monitoring and failing safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Test your automation for problems and set up a weekly check.
This lesson builds toward: Before and after switching your automation on, you will test it with odd inputs, turn on failure alerts and plan a weekly check, so it stops and alerts you when something goes wrong.
Automations break: an app changes, a form question is renamed, a password expires, or the AI gives a strange answer. Test with odd inputs: an empty field, a very long message, a message in another language, a rude message.
Set it to fail safely: if something goes wrong, the automation should stop and tell you, not send a half-finished message. Most tools can email you when a run fails; turn that on.
Once a week, look at the log: how many runs, how many failed, and two or three AI drafts. Count the minutes saved. If it is causing more work than it saves, change it or switch it off.
Step by step:
- Test with an empty field, a very long message and an unusual message.
- Turn on failure alerts.
- Make sure a failure stops the run instead of sending something.
- Each week, check runs, failures and a few AI drafts.
- Keep, change or switch off based on time saved.
Words to know:
- Fail safely: when something goes wrong, stop and alert a person instead of doing something harmful.
- Run: one time the automation starts and works through its steps.
Try it now: Final task: test your automation with three odd inputs, turn on failure alerts, and write your one-page record: map, trigger and actions, AI instruction, approval step, test results and weekly check.
You can now build, guard, test and monitor an AI automation for your business.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Workflow map Steps are missing or not marked. Every step from start to finish, marked copying, decision or writing. Notes how long each step takes by hand today. Trigger and actions The trigger or actions are unclear. One clear trigger and a list of actions, with the AI step and approval marked. Field mapping is written for every piece of information. Working automation It does not run, or was tested with real customer data. Form to spreadsheet plus notification works, tested with made-up data. Notes the free-plan limits checked on the tool's own pricing page. AI step and guardrails AI can send to customers or act on risky steps without approval. AI drafts go to the owner for approval; guardrail list with five approval items. The AI instruction has clear rules and private fields are kept out of the AI step. Testing and monitoring Fewer than three tests, or no failure alert. Three odd-input tests, failure alerts on and a weekly check written. Weekly check includes minutes saved and a rule for when to switch it off. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Testing with unusual data, such as an empty field
check.why: Odd inputs show how the automation handles problems.

check.q: Your weekly check shows five failed runs. What do you do?
options: Find the cause, fix it and test again
check.why: Monitoring is for catching and fixing failures.
